entities.name: Marcus Valerius Messalla Appianus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Valerius Messalla Appianus, a scion of the distinguished Valeria gens, served as an ordinary consul in 12 BCE during the formative years of Emperor Augustus's reign. His brief but high-ranking career underscores the continued importance of aristocratic lineage and established political networks in the early Roman Principate, even as traditional republican institutions were being reshaped by imperial power. Appianus's consulship, shared with Publius Sulpicius Quirinius, placed him at the apex of Roman civic administration, overseeing the city and its vast empire in a critical period of transition from republic to empire.

Born into a prominent family, Appianus's ascent to the consulship in 12 BCE marked him as a promising figure within the Augustan political establishment. The Fasti Consulares record his tenure alongside Quirinius, a military commander who would later gain fame for his governorship of Syria and his role in the census mentioned in the Gospel of Luke. While specific details of Appianus's actions during his consulship are scarce in surviving records, his office would have involved presiding over the Senate, overseeing judicial proceedings, and engaging in public works, all under the watchful eye of Augustus, who carefully managed the distribution of such prestigious magistracies to loyal and capable individuals. His likely adoption into the Valerii Messallae family further cemented his elite status, enabling his rapid political advancement.
